claims.text: The proposed approach isolates lattice thermal conductivity from electronic heat transport.
The approach combines DFT calculations, temperature-adjusted Debye-temperature estimates, and force-constant variations.
The proposed approach will predict lattice thermal conductivity within approximately ±20% error.
The proposed approach will be more accurate than earlier models that conflate lattice and electronic transport.
High-purity, defect-minimized HfNbTaTiZr is the intended sample state.
Samples containing approximately 1 wt.% oxygen may be used for high-temperature validation.
Below 200 K, lattice and electronic contributions can be experimentally separated.
DFT-derived elastic moduli, Debye-temperature estimates, and force-constant variations are proxies for atomic interactions in near-perfect HfNbTaTiZr.
Using the proposed structural mediators will capture lattice-dynamical behavior more accurately.
Decoupling lattice and electronic conduction will mitigate errors caused by conflating the two channels.
Low-temperature lattice thermal-conductivity predictions will agree with independent measurements within ±20%.
High-temperature total-conductivity trends will be captured more accurately than by previous composite models.
Earlier predictive methodologies combined lattice and electronic contributions while assuming perfect, defect-free bulk structures.
Earlier methodologies typically deviate more from isolated lattice measurements than the proposed approach.
The proposed approach is applicable from approximately 50 K to 1200 K.
The approach is expected to become unreliable for oxygen contents well above 1 wt.% because of impurity or defect scattering.
Additional quantum effects may limit the approach at extremely low temperatures.
The anticipated ±20% error margin is based on current supporting observations.

contradictions.description: The intervention specifies a model of the lattice contribution independently of electronic transport, but the predicted outcome and falsification test require prediction of high-temperature total conductivity without specifying how the electronic contribution is modeled or added.
